analysis.one_liner: Diverts two percentage points of Social Security payroll taxes into personal investment accounts while phasing in benefit changes to extend solvency.
analysis.headline: The bill had a Republican sponsor and six bipartisan cosponsors — three Democrats and three Republicans — but was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a personal savings account for every worker born after 1937, funded by redirecting two percentage points of the Social Security payroll tax (employees would pay 4.2% instead of 6.2%, with the difference going to their account), plus up to $2,000 a year in voluntary contributions matched by a federal tax credit. Children born in 1995 or later would get government-funded 'KidSave' accounts: $1,000 at birth and $500 on each of their first five birthdays. To pay for this and extend the program's solvency, it would gradually shrink traditional benefits for higher earners, reduce annual inflation adjustments, make early retirement less generous, raise the wage cap on taxable earnings, and cut transfers from Social Security to the Medicare trust fund. It also would improve widow and widower benefits and let early retirees work without losing benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers born after 1937 would own a personal investment account funded by their own payroll money, administered like the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, and could leave any remaining balance to heirs. Families with children born in 1995 or later would receive government seed money in KidSave accounts. Widows and widowers would get a more generous benefit formula, and early retirees could work without having benefits withheld.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers born after 1937 and young children

how_it_helps.text: The employee share of the Social Security payroll tax would drop from 6.2% to 4.2%, with the 2-point difference deposited into the worker's own account, and workers could add up to $2,000 a year that would be matched through a federal tax credit.

Every child born on or after January 1, 1995 would get a KidSave account funded by the Treasury: $1,000 at birth for those born in 2001 or later, and $500 on each of the first five birthdays for those born 1995 or later.
The earnings test would be eliminated for people who retire early, meaning they could keep working and drawing wages without having their Social Security checks reduced.
Widows' and widowers' benefits would be recalculated to the greater of the deceased spouse's benefit or a share of the couple's joint benefit, phasing up to 75% by 2010.

Accounts would be managed by a board within the Social Security Administration in the same manner as the Thrift Savings Plan for federal employees, a low-cost, tightly regulated structure, and kept off the federal budget.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the trust fund would lose two points of payroll revenue, so traditional benefits would shrink over time: the benefit formula would gradually flatten (cutting benefits most for higher earners), annual inflation adjustments would be trimmed by up to 0.33 percentage points for every CPI-indexed federal program, early retirement would carry a larger permanent reduction, all working years would count in benefit calculations, the wage cap on taxable earnings would rise, and transfers from Social Security to the Medicare hospital trust fund would be phased down 10 percentage points a year after 2004.
analysis.who_pays_short: Future retirees, the Medicare trust fund

drawbacks.text: Money deposited into a personal account is not on top of traditional Social Security — the bill would reduce a retiree's traditional benefit by an actuarial offset equal to the amounts credited to the account, so account gains partly claw back guaranteed benefits.

The inflation adjustment would be cut by 0.1 to 0.33 percentage points a year, and that cut would apply to every federal program indexed to the Consumer Price Index and to tax provisions, not just Social Security — a slow but permanent benefit cut for current retirees and other beneficiaries.
The bill would make early retirement less generous, raising the actuarial reduction from 5/9 of one percent per month to 25/36 of one percent for people turning 62 in 2005 or later.
By 2010, all years of a worker's life would count in the benefit computation, which lowers benefits for people with years of low or zero earnings, such as caregivers and seasonal workers.
Account balances would be exposed to investment risk, though the bill limits choices and instructs default designations to balance maximizing returns against minimizing risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a genuine bipartisan compromise: workers would gain real, bequeathable personal accounts and children would get seed savings, while the solvency fixes are progressive, falling hardest on higher earners and later retirees rather than on today's poor or disabled beneficiaries, who are expressly shielded from the offsets and formula changes. But the costs are real and spread widely — every beneficiary would absorb a smaller cost-of-living increase each year, early retirees would take a bigger haircut, and Medicare's hospital fund would lose transfers — and the accounts' apparent gains are partly offset against guaranteed benefits. Whether it was a good deal depended heavily on market returns that no one could guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced in June 2000, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Judd Gregg introduced the Bipartisan Social Security Reform Act of 2000 on June 22, 2000, joined by six cosponsors — three Democrats (Kerrey, Breaux, Robb) and three Republicans (Grassley, Thompson, Thomas).
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of any kind in the chamber.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it never became law, Social Security continued unchanged: current beneficiaries kept their full cost-of-living adjustments, the Medicare trust fund kept its transfers, and the push for personally directed accounts stalled. Higher earners were spared both the rising taxable wage cap and the steepest benefit cuts, while workers who wanted personal accounts got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of Social Security as it was

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from birth — one Republican sponsor with three Republican and three Democratic cosponsors — but it never reached a vote, so no roll call exists to show where the wider chambers stood.

industries.note: Unlike most privatization plans, the bill would route accounts through a government-run fund board modeled on the federal Thrift Savings Plan, keeping fees low and limiting the industry's role at first — but the board would be required to study and recommend expanding private investment options and rollovers, a door to larger fee business later. Workers, not the industry, would own the account assets.

The bill would reset the taxable wage cap at 84.5% of total covered wages, raising the earnings ceiling subject to payroll tax, and its formula changes cut traditional benefits most for higher earners. Their added contributions would help fund the solvency fix that protects everyone else.

industries.industry: Medicare hospital financing (Hospital Insurance Trust Fund)
industries.note: The bill would phase down the transfers Social Security makes to the Medicare trust fund by 10 percentage points a year after 2004, tightening Medicare's financing in order to shore up Social Security.
